questions.question_text: A dataset has a mean of $\mu = 58$ and a standard deviation of $\sigma = 9$. What is the raw value with a $z$-score of $1.4$?

options.why: Subtracted $z\sigma$ from the mean even though $z$ is positive, placing the value below the mean.
Stopped at $z\sigma = 1.4 \times 9$ and forgot to add the mean.
Added the z-score itself to the mean instead of multiplying it by the standard deviation first.

questions.question_text: A dataset has a mean of $\mu = 210$ and a standard deviation of $\sigma = 16$. What is the raw value with a $z$-score of $-0.75$?

options.why: Ignored the negative sign on $z$ and added $12$ instead of subtracting it.
Subtracted the z-score itself from the mean instead of multiplying it by the standard deviation first.
Subtracted a whole standard deviation, treating any negative z-score as one deviation below the mean.

questions.question_text: The marks in an examination have a mean of $64$ and a standard deviation of $7$. What mark is $2.5$ standard deviations below the mean?

options.why: Added instead of subtracting, giving the mark $2.5$ standard deviations above the mean.
Subtracted $2.5$ from the mean instead of $2.5$ standard deviations.
Subtracted a single standard deviation, ignoring the factor of $2.5$.

questions.solution_text:
$2.5$ standard deviations below the mean means $z = -2.5$.
$x = \mu + z\sigma$
$= 64 + (-2.5) \times 7$
$= 64 - 17.5$
$= 46.5$

questions.question_text: The lengths of a batch of bolts have a mean of $24.6$ cm and a standard deviation of $1.8$ cm. What is the length of a bolt with a $z$-score of $1.5$?

options.why: Subtracted $z\sigma$ from the mean even though $z$ is positive.
Added the z-score itself to the mean instead of multiplying it by the standard deviation first.
Stopped at $z\sigma = 1.5 \times 1.8$ and forgot to add the mean.

questions.question_text: In a dataset with a standard deviation of $6$, the value $35$ has a $z$-score of $-2.5$. What is the mean?

options.why: Used $\mu = x + z\sigma$, subtracting $15$ instead of adding it, so the mean ends up below a value that is known to be below the mean.
Divided the value by the z-score instead of using $\mu = x - z\sigma$.
Added one standard deviation to the value, ignoring the size of the z-score.

questions.question_text: In a dataset with a mean of $71$, the value $95$ has a $z$-score of $3$. What is the standard deviation?

options.why: Stopped at the difference $95 - 71$ without dividing by the z-score.
Multiplied the difference by the z-score instead of dividing by it.
Divided the raw value by the z-score instead of dividing the difference $x - \mu$ by it.

questions.question_text: In a dataset with a mean of $59$, the value $44$ has a $z$-score of $-2.5$. What is the standard deviation?

options.why: Divided $-15$ by $2.5$, dropping the negative sign on the z-score; a standard deviation is never negative.
Multiplied the difference by the z-score instead of dividing by it.
Stopped at the size of the difference $44 - 59$ without dividing by the z-score.

questions.question_text: In a dataset the value $84$ has a $z$-score of $2$ and the value $66$ has a $z$-score of $-1$. What is the mean?

options.why: Averaged the two values, which ignores that they are different distances from the mean.
Found $\sigma = 6$ correctly but then subtracted it from $66$ instead of adding it.
Found $\sigma = 6$ correctly but subtracted only one standard deviation from $84$, treating $z = 2$ as one deviation.

questions.solution_text:
$x = \mu + z\sigma$ for each value gives
$84 = \mu + 2\sigma$
$66 = \mu - \sigma$
Subtracting the second equation from the first,
$18 = 3\sigma$
$\sigma = 6$
Substituting into the second equation,
$66 = \mu - 6$
$\mu = 72$
